The t-test compared **two** groups. Biology is full of **three-or-more** group

still `lm(Y ~ X)`, just with a **categorical** X. That is **one-way ANOVA**.

# How to Use These Slides — Predict · Type · Run

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
I lecture through the material, then you open the skeleton script and run the
code yourself.

**For every code block, do three things:**

1.  **Predict** — before it runs, say what you think the output will be
2.  **Type** it out by hand — do not copy-paste
3.  **Run** it and compare to your prediction
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-note
**✅ Why bother? (the evidence)**

- With three groups it is tempting to just read off the tallest box. Predicting
  the F first makes you reason about between- vs. within-group variance.
- Typing `type = 2` yourself in `Anova()` is what makes you notice it is there.
- You will meet `anova()`, `aov()` and `Anova()` in one lecture. Typing each
  one is how they stop blurring together.
:::
::::
:::::

# Why Not Just Run Many t-Tests?

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
With **3 groups** you would need **3** t-tests (A–B, A–C, B–C). With 4 groups,
**6** tests.

Every test at α = 0.05 has a **5% chance of a false positive**. Run several and
those risks **stack up**:

- 3 tests → ~**14%** chance of at least one false positive
- 6 tests → ~**26%**

ANOVA asks the question **once**, holding the overall error rate at 0.05.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
**The multiple-comparisons problem**

More tests = more chances to be fooled by noise. ANOVA is the single, honest
test for "do *any* of these groups differ?"
:::

📖 W&S §15.1 — why a single test
::::
:::::

# What One-Way ANOVA Asks

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
One **numeric response (Y)** across the levels of one **categorical predictor (X)**.

| | Hypothesis |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------|
| **H₀ — null** | all group means are equal ($\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3$) |
| **Hₐ — alternate** | **at least one** group mean differs |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

Note what Hₐ does *not* say: it does **not** tell you *which* group differs —
that is Set 3, next lecture.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**Our question today:**

Do the three penguin **species** differ in **body mass**?

- Y = `body_mass_g`
- X = `species` (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo)
::::
:::::

# The F-Statistic — Between vs. Within

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
$$F = \frac{\text{variance BETWEEN groups}}{\text{variance WITHIN groups}}$$

- **Between** — how far apart the group means are
- **Within** — how much the individuals scatter inside each group

**Big F** → the groups are far apart *relative to* their internal noise → small
*p*-value.

**F ≈ 1** → the spread between groups is no bigger than the spread within them
→ no real difference.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-note
**✅ Key idea**

ANOVA is a **signal-to-noise ratio** — the same shape as *t*. The "signal" is
the gap between group means; the "noise" is the within-group scatter.
:::

📖 W&S §15.1–15.2
::::
:::::

# Meet the Data — Palmer Penguins

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r load-libs-15}
# Load packages at the top — always -------------------
library(tidyverse)      # wrangling + ggplot2
library(palmerpenguins) # the penguins data
library(car)            # Anova()
```

```{r load-data-15}
# Drop rows missing mass or species -------------------
penguins_df <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g, species)

penguins_df %>% count(species)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**Three species, one field station:** body mass (g) of penguins at Palmer
Station, Antarctica.

- `drop_na()` removes rows with missing mass
- `count(species)` gives the sample size per group

::: callout-important
The groups are **unbalanced** — 151, 68 and 123 birds. That is why we care
which sums of squares `Anova()` uses.
:::
::::
:::::

:::: {.column width="60%"}
R 4.5 added its **own** `penguins` to base R, with **shorter column names**:


# Explore First — Boxplot by Species

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r boxplot-15}
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of penguin body mass in grams by species (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo) with jittered individual points overlaid, showing Gentoo penguins noticeably heavier than the other two species, which sit at about the same level."
mass_box_plot <- penguins_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body Mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

mass_box_plot
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-note
**🔮 Predict first:** all three species, or just one? Which is heaviest?
:::

**Always plot before you test.**

- Gentoo sits well above the other two
- Adelie and Chinstrap are **almost on top of each other** — hold that thought
- The box heights are **not** all equal — hold that one too (Set 2)
- The order is **alphabetical**, not by mass
::::
:::::

# `species` Is a Factor — and Factors Have an Order

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r factor-inspect-15}
class(penguins_df$species)   # "factor"
levels(penguins_df$species)  # the stored order
```

- A **factor** is a categorical column with a fixed, *ordered* set of **levels**
- `ggplot` (and `lm`) draw and model groups in **level order**
- The default level order is **alphabetical** — almost never what you want
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-note
**✅ Key idea**

Alphabetical order hides the pattern. Ordering the groups by the thing you are
testing — here, body mass — makes the boxplot tell the story at a glance.
:::

`forcats` (the `fct_*` family) ships with `library(tidyverse)`.
::::
:::::

# Order the Boxplot by Body Mass — `fct_reorder()`

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r fct-reorder-15}
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: "The same penguin body-mass boxplot with species reordered by median mass from lightest to heaviest: Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo. The order is now data-driven rather than alphabetical."
penguins_df %>%
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, body_mass_g,
                               .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(x = "Species (ordered by median mass)",
       y = "Body Mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
- `fct_reorder(f, x, .fun = median)` — reorder factor `f` by a summary of `x`
- Do it **inside `mutate()`**, then plot the result
- Here the alphabetical order happens to already be the mass order — but now it
  is that way **on purpose**, and it will hold for data where it does not

::: callout-tip
The full `forcats` family — rename levels, merge them, lump rare ones — is in
**Common Code 15 · Factors**. Today we need *ordering*, and `fct_relevel()` for
the baseline in a moment.
:::
::::
:::::

# State the Hypotheses — Before Any Code

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
**H₀:** $\mu_{\text{Adelie}} = \mu_{\text{Chinstrap}} = \mu_{\text{Gentoo}}$

**Hₐ:** at least one species mean differs from the others

**α = 0.05**

That is the whole hypothesis set. There is **one** test and **one** *p*-value,
no matter how many groups you have.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
Hₐ is deliberately vague. "At least one differs" is all the F-test can tell
you. If you want to name the species, you need the follow-up tests — Set 3.
:::
::::
:::::

# Fit the Model — `lm()`

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r fit-15}
# ANOVA is a linear model with a categorical X --------
mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)
```

- `lm(Y ~ X)` — the *same* function call as regression
- When `X` is **categorical**, that linear model **is** a one-way ANOVA
- Fitting the model and **reading a table from it** are two separate steps
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-note
**✅ Key idea**

You do not write anything different to get an ANOVA instead of a regression.
`lm()` looks at the class of `X` and codes it for you. One function, two tests.
:::

📖 W&S §15.2
::::
:::::

# What `lm()` Did With a Factor — the Baseline

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r coef-15}
coef(mass_model)
```

- `(Intercept)` is the mean of the **first level** — Adelie
- The other coefficients are **differences from Adelie**
- Chinstrap is +32 g; Gentoo is +1375 g
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
This is **treatment coding** (`contr.treatment`) — R's default. Each group is
compared with a baseline group.

::: callout-note
Remember this phrase: *treatment coding compares every group with the first
level.* It comes back in two slides when we ask `Anova()` for Type III.
:::
::::
:::::

# Change the Baseline — `fct_relevel()`

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r fct-relevel-15}
# Make Gentoo the reference instead -------------------
penguins_relevel <- penguins_df %>%
  mutate(species = fct_relevel(species, "Gentoo"))

mass_model_gentoo <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species,
                        data = penguins_relevel)
coef(mass_model_gentoo)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
- `fct_relevel(species, "Gentoo")` moves Gentoo to the front → the coefficients
  are now differences **from Gentoo**

::: callout-important
Releveling changes **which comparisons the coefficients show**. It does **not**
change the overall **F** or *p*-value — "do any means differ?" is the same
question whichever group you call the baseline.
:::

Use it to make the baseline a group your reader cares about — a control, a
reference site.
::::
:::::

# Read the Table — `aov()` and `summary()`

::: callout-note
**🔮 Predict first:** The boxplot was very separated. Predict the *p*-value —
nearer 0.5, 0.05, or far below 0.001?
:::

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r aov-15}
# The classic ANOVA table -----------------------------
mass_aov <- aov(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)
summary(mass_aov)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**Reading the table:**

| Column | Meaning |
|-----------|-------------------------------|
| `Df` | groups − 1, then residual df |
| `Sum Sq` | variation explained / left over |
| `F value` | between ÷ within |
| `Pr(>F)` | the *p*-value for H₀ |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

*p* < 0.05 → **reject H₀** → at least one species differs.
::::
:::::

# Three Function Names, One Idea

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
| Call | Package | Gives you |
|-------------------------|---------|----------------------------|
| `aov(y ~ x)` + `summary()` | base R | the classic ANOVA table |
| `anova(model)` | base R | **Type I** (sequential) table |
| `Anova(model)` | **car** | **Type II** table (the default) |
| `Anova(model, type = 3)` | **car** | **Type III** table |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,16,50]"}

Lowercase `anova()` and capital `Anova()` are **different functions from
different packages**. R will not guess which you meant.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
`Anova()` lives in **car**. Without `library(car)` you get

```
could not find function "Anova"
```

With one predictor all four of these give the **same F for `species`**. The
differences only bite once you have two or more predictors — which is exactly
why we build the habit now.
:::
::::
:::::

# `car::Anova()` — Type II Is the Default

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r carAnova-15}
# No type argument = Type II --------------------------
Anova(mass_model)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**Why Type II?**

- Our groups have **different n** (unbalanced)
- Type I is **order-dependent** — swap the predictors and the table changes
- Type II is **order-independent**, and it is the habit you want before two-way
  ANOVA, where the type genuinely changes the answer

`Anova(mass_model, type = 2)` is the same thing, written out.
::::
:::::

# Type III Needs a Different Contrast Coding

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
Type III sums of squares are only meaningful when the factors are coded so each
group is compared with the **grand mean** — `contr.sum` — not with a baseline
group (`contr.treatment`).

```{r contrasts-check-15}
# What is R using right now? --------------------------
getOption("contrasts")
```

That is R's default: **treatment** coding for unordered factors, **polynomial**
for ordered ones.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
**The rule**

`Anova(model, type = 3)` wants

``` r
c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")
```

Ask for Type III on a treatment-coded model and `car` will still print a table
— it just will not be the Type III test you think it is.
:::
::::
:::::

# Switch to `contr.sum` — and Refit

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r contrasts-sum-15}
# 1. change the option -------------------------------
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

# 2. REFIT the model under the new coding ------------
mass_model_sum <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species,
                     data = penguins_df)

# 3. now Type III means what it says -----------------
Anova(mass_model_sum, type = 3)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
**Step 2 is not optional**

A model stores the coding it was **fitted** with. Change the option and reuse
the old model and nothing happens:

``` r
mass_model$contrasts
#> $species
#> [1] "contr.treatment"
```

Set the option, **then** `lm()` again.
:::
::::
:::::

# And Switch Back — Always

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r contrasts-back-15}
# Put R back the way you found it ---------------------
options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

getOption("contrasts")
```

`options()` is **global and sticky** — it stays changed for the rest of your
session and affects every model you fit afterwards, including ones in code you
wrote weeks ago.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-tip
**The pattern to memorize**

``` r
options(contrasts =
  c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
m <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
Anova(m, type = 3)
options(contrasts =
  c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))
```

Set → refit → test → set back. Four lines, in that order, every time.
:::
::::
:::::

# What Actually Changed? Only the Intercept Row

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
**Treatment coding, `type = 3`:**

```
            Sum Sq  Df F value
(Intercept) 2.07e9   1  9676.9
species     1.47e8   2   343.6
Residuals   7.24e7 339
```

**Sum coding, `type = 3`:**

```
            Sum Sq  Df F value
(Intercept) 5.31e9   1 24859.3
species     1.47e8   2   343.6
Residuals   7.24e7 339
```
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
The `species` row is **identical** — 343.6 either way. Only `(Intercept)`
moved, because the intercept means something different under each coding
(Adelie's mean vs. the grand mean).

::: callout-note
**✅ So why bother?**

With **one** factor, you cannot see the difference in the row you care about.
With **two** factors and an interaction, you can — the predictor rows change
too. Learn the four-line pattern on the easy case, so it is automatic on the
hard one.
:::
::::
:::::

# Which Table Should You Report?

| Situation | Use |
|---------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| One factor, any design | any of them — they agree. `Anova(model)` is a fine habit |
| Two+ factors, **balanced** | all three types agree |
| Two+ factors, **unbalanced** | **Type II** for main effects with no interaction |
| Interaction you want to keep in | **Type III**, with `contr.sum` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

::: callout-tip
In this course: report **`Anova(model)`** (Type II) unless you have a specific
reason. Know the Type III recipe because reviewers, SPSS and SAS users ask for
it by name.
:::

# Report the Result

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r report-15}
# The numbers you need, in one table ------------------
Anova(mass_model)
```

> *"Body mass differed significantly among the three penguin species (one-way
> ANOVA: F(2, 339) = 343.6, p < 0.001)."*
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**Always include:**

- the test (one-way ANOVA)
- **F**, **both df**, the ***p*-value**
- the direction, once you know it

**Never** write "p = 0.000" — write "p < 0.001".

::: callout-important
Notice what the sentence does **not** say: *which* species differ. It cannot —
and neither can you, yet.
:::
::::
:::::

# What We Learned Today

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
**Concepts:**

- Many t-tests inflate the false-positive rate — **ANOVA asks once**
- **F** = between-group ÷ within-group variance
- A **factor**'s level order sets the plot order and the model baseline
- ANOVA is a linear model with a categorical predictor
- Type I / II / III differ in how they allocate sums of squares; **Type III
  needs `contr.sum`**, and the model must be **refit**

**R skills:**

- `fct_reorder()`, `fct_relevel()`
- `lm(Y ~ group)`, `coef()`
- `aov()` + `summary()`, `anova()`, `car::Anova()`
- `options(contrasts = ...)` — set, refit, test, set back
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**References:**

- 📖 W&S Ch. 15 — ANOVA
- 📖 [R4DS Ch. 16 — Factors](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/factors)

**Up next — Lecture 20:**

- **Set 2 — the assumptions.** We reported *p* < 0.001 today without earning
  it. Are the residuals normal? Are the variances equal? One of those answers
  is going to be **no**.
- **Set 3 — the follow-up tests.** Adelie and Chinstrap looked identical on the
  boxplot. We find out whether they are.
::::
